issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, this appraisal is a poor thematic fit because it implies an interpersonal perpetrator threat ('who will harm you') rather than danger from impersonal environmental forces. The rest of the profile is built around disaster-related ongoing danger/hypervigilance and intrusive reliving, so this item stands out as clinically incongruent with the specified trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe classic fear-based re-experiencing and hypervigilance, but there is no accompanying content suggesting perpetration, moral injury, or a specific action during the disaster that would plausibly drive a strong violated-values appraisal.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' could occur after a disaster, but here it sits awkwardly with the otherwise generic fear/reliving profile. There are no memory or threat items about failing to protect family, losing dependents, or role-related guilt, so this item lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'I need to stay alert' while trying to sleep is more characteristic of an ongoing human threat context than of a completed natural disaster, especially when paired with scanning exits and staying near exits in all buildings. Taken together, these threat items imply anticipation of intentional attack or entrapment rather than the specific threat structure suggested by the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is not impossible, but it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile for a 65-year-old married male retail worker with natural-disaster trauma. The rest of the profile centers on ongoing danger, hypervigilance, and intrusive reliving; this item instead implies a specific role-based self-evaluation that is not supported by the other selected appraisals, memory, threat, or coping items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'Other-Blame Rumination' sits awkwardly with a natural-disaster trauma profile. Blame can occur, but this item specifically focuses on dwelling on what other people have done to me, whereas the rest of the profile describes threat and reliving linked to impersonal environmental danger rather than interpersonal harm or betrayal. Without any corroborating appraisal or memory content involving preventable human actions, this item is clinically hard to reconcile.

vignette: Malik was twenty-eight when the hurricane surged through the coastal county, a wall of wind and rising water that swallowed the retail district where he worked. He had been stacking crates in the back of a department store when the glass façade cracked and a sheet of the building gave way. Water rushed in with a roar, sweeping carts and boxes like driftwood. He remembers the sudden, breathless weight of it, the way the current pulled at his ankles, the deafening strike of a signboard against the floor. He climbed onto a high counter, clutching a metal display rack for stability, as the storm raged outside. The water did not recede for hours, and by the time rescue came, the store was submerged, the ceiling dripping, the air thick with the smell of wet plaster and salt. In the months that followed, the experience did not settle into his mind as something finished. He found his memories replaying like a film that plays over and over. When he closed his eyes at night, he saw the same water surging past the counters, the same glass fragmenting in slow motion. He would sit up in bed, feeling like it is happening right now rather than something over. The memory felt present, not past, and the weight of that permanence settled over him. He had come to believe he is permanently changed for the worse, his body still carrying the tension of that trapped climb. What startled him most was the suddenness of it. A dropped box in the aisle, a gust of wind against the store doors, even the sound of rain on the parking lot roof, would pull him back into that moment. He is superalert or watchful or on guard, and he has come to believe the world is a dangerous place. What frightened him most was not the storm itself, but how easily the ground could give way again, how thin the boundary between safety and threat had become. Now sixty-five and still working as a retail worker at a neighborhood grocery, Malik moves through his days with a quiet intensity. He scans for exits as soon as he enters any room or building, his eyes tracking the automatic doors, the side doors, the stairwells. He stays near the exit, positioning himself by the front doors so he can feel the steady flow of air and the clear path to the street. When the store grows loud or the aisles feel too enclosed, he distracts himself with something else, focusing intently on the price tags, the scanner beeps, the rhythm of his own breathing. He is constantly scanning his surroundings, his posture coiled. The scanning, the staying close to the door, and the distraction run alongside each other in his daily routine. At home, the sleep vigilance sits beside him. He has difficulty falling asleep because he needs to stay alert, listening for the hum of the refrigerator, the creak of the house settling, the distant rumble of a truck on the highway. Over weeks and months, these habits hardened into steady patterns. He avoids the back porch during heavy rain, preferring the interior rooms where the walls feel solid. He no longer takes the long route to the stockroom, opting instead for the shorter path that keeps him near the front. The consequence is subtle but tangible: he misses the slower rhythm of the full day, the chance conversations with regulars, the quiet satisfaction of a completed shift, because he is often watching the doors, waiting for a shift in the weather, a sudden gust, a familiar surge. Malik finally sought help after a Tuesday morning when a heavy downstorm triggered a brief power flicker at the grocery. For a moment, the lights dimmed, and the automatic doors slid open with a sudden rush of wind. He stood frozen near the entrance, his heart drumming, the store dissolving into the memory of that flooded floor. He walked to the cashier’s desk and asked if they had a community health clinic nearby. He was not looking for a cure, but for a way to understand why his body still reacted as though the water were rising again. What he feared most was that the danger was permanent, that he was irrevocably altered, and that he would spend the rest of his days scanning the horizon for another storm. What he hoped for was simply to feel, once again, that the past was past, and that he could step through a door without bracing.
